newsitem.title: GERMANY: German mobile phone firms ready new price war.
newsitem.headline: German mobile phone firms ready new price war.

text.p: German mobile phone operators and resellers will unveil deep cuts in charges this week as a price war breaks out ahead of the year-end shopping season, industry officials said on Monday.

Mannesmann Mobilfunk, the digital cellular network owned by Mannesmann and AirTouch Communications of the United States, is expected to announce on Wednesday sharp cuts in both monthly charges and some services from November.

The new round of price cuts will mark a grab for market share in the residential market, which makes up an increasing part of total connections, and comes as the government ends bidding on Tuesday for a fourth mobile phone licence.
Industry officials said Mannesmann is expected to launch an aggressive marketing and advertising campaign and underbid recent price reductions by Deutsche Telekom.
Most German resellers are expected to follow suit.

Accounting for 30 percent to 40 percent of Germany's 4.5 million digital cellular subscribers, resellers repackage the services of the big three mobile phone companies -- Mannesmann's D2, Deutsche Telekom's D1 and the E-Plus network -- and add services such as ticket ordering.

"Our strategy is to pass on every price cut from the mobile phone operators one-to-one to our customers," said Henning Ohlsson, marketing manager at Motorola's Tel-Co unit, a small reseller with some 85,000 subscribers.
"This is going to give a real boost to the whole market ahead of the Christmas season so that we will see real growth in the residential market."
Deutsche Telekom last week stunned its main competitors by slashing the monthly charge for its D1 network to 29 marks ($18.94) from 49, beginning November
Telekom also broke with a long-standing industry habit by deciding to no longer include a mobile phone free-of-charge or at a discounted price with every new connection.
Instead, the company hopes it will be able to cut costs by decoupling the sale of the basic connection and the telephone.
It also said that a secondhand market for mobile phones could emerge and estimated there were around one million used phones on the market that were not in active service.

Telekom's price cuts appear to be a defensive move because it has been losing ground to Mannesmann, which originally expected two million new connections this year. That number was already reached in August and industry sources say D2 is winning 80,000 new customers a month.
Telekom's price cuts have angered some of its rivals, who said there was no reason to cut prices now.

"We will almost certainly announce something on Wednesday. But the whole thing is unnecessary. Why should we lower prices when customers are lining up at the door?" said Ralf Breuer, spokesman for Debitel, Germany's largest reseller.
Debitel, owned by Daimler-Benz Interservices AG and Metro AG, has some 750,000 subscribers in Germany and another 200,000 in neighbouring countries.
E-Plus, owned by Veba, Thyssen, BellSouth and Vodafone, was the one company that did not appear to be preparing reductions in charges.
"We don't see any real need to do anything right now," said Dietrich Gemmel, director of E-Plus corporate development. "We will wait and see what D2 does."
